1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.name: Caro–Kann Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Releases the tension and denies White the broad two-pawn centre and frees d5 for Black's pieces. Black gets a flexible, solid structure and a bishop that can come out before the pawns close it in.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze System
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.background: Originated by Bukhuti Gurgenidze, this variation led to a rise in the popularity of 3.Nd2 during the 1970s.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure d4, keeping the d5 tension instead of exchanging. Black allows White to take space in the centre and on the kingside, but builds a counterattack on the long diagonal against the white centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Campomanes Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the tension, hoping for a quiet game. White can drive the knight back with a pawn, gaining space and a closed centre for which Black may not have prepared, so Black ends up passive for little.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Gurgenidze Counterattack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 b5.strategy: Hopes to drive the knight from c3 with ...b4, but loosens the queenside and spends a move on a pawn. White stops the idea with a3 and keeps a lead in development, so Black is left with weaknesses; it works only as a surprise at club level.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Main Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight takes a central post and White keeps a healthy pawn structure with a small lead in space. Black's c8-bishop is free to develop, but Black has to find a good way to deal with the centralised knight.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.f3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Rasa-Studier Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.f3.strategy: A gambit that offers a second pawn to open lines and develop with tempo, hoping to attack a king still in the centre. White does not get full compensation for the pawn, but the lines can be sharp and punish careless defence.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Bc4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: von Hennig Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop against f7 and prepares the same pawn sacrifice with f3, after which the play usually converges with the other gambit. White does not get full compensation for the pawn, so Black can take it and defend calmly.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5.background: Also called the Capablanca Variation, after the Cuban world champion José Raúl Capablanca. It was long considered to represent best play for both sides.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can close it in, and attacks the centralised knight. Black keeps the pawn structure healthy and contests d4 later with ...c5, a solid set-up with few weaknesses that long counted as best play.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Karpov Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7.background: It was once named after the first world champion Wilhelm Steinitz, who played it, and is also called the Smyslov Variation, after Vasily Smyslov, who played a number of notable games with it. It is named after Anatoly Karpov because it appeared quite often in his repertoire.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7.strategy: Develops a knight instead of the bishop, aiming to trade White's centralised knight without damaging the pawn structure. The cost is a slower bishop and more room for White in the centre, so White often looks for kingside pressure.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6.strategy: Challenges the knight on e4 and offers the trade, at the price of a damaged structure: if White takes on f6, Black must recapture with a pawn and accept doubled f-pawns. Black gets quick development and a playable game in return.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 h6.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Finnish Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 h6.strategy: Plays the ...h6 of the Classical set-up in advance, so the bishop can later retreat to h7 and avoid being harassed on the kingside. It costs a tempo in a position where White develops freely, so White keeps a small edge.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..strategy: Answers the attack on the knight with an attack on the bishop, so Black has to decide where the bishop belongs. White keeps all the pieces, and the knight covers h5, which lets an h-pawn advance harass the bishop later.

Sidesteps the bishop by jumping to g5, from where the knight eyes f7 and h7. Nothing real follows, since both are covered, and the knight stands offside, where Black can drive it back with a pawn move. A rare, harmless alternative.
A quiet retreat: the knight goes back to c3 and keeps the centre intact. It costs a tempo and gives up the active post on e4, so Black completes development without difficulty.

Retreats out of the knight's attack to g6, where the f7 and h7 pawns protect the bishop. It keeps the bishop on the diagonal towards d3, so a bishop exchange stays possible; the price is that White's h-pawn can now go after it.

Steps back along the other diagonal instead of to g6, keeping the bishop in the centre and out of reach of a kingside pawn advance. It gives up the b1-h7 diagonal, though, and White can gain time by attacking the bishop on e6.
Attacks the queen, but the bishop is undefended and White simply takes it: the queen wins a piece for nothing.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Classical Variation, Main Line
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..strategy: The main line: it threatens h5, which would trap the bishop, because every square it could go to is covered and the h7 pawn blocks its retreat. Black has to make room at once, and White gains kingside space and the initiative, though the advanced pawn can become a target in the endgame.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Classical Variation, Flohr Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..strategy: Heads for f4 to challenge the bishop on g6; from there the knight would also eye d5 and e6, and an exchange would give White the bishop pair. Until it arrives the knight stands on the rim, which gives Black time to organise the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Classical Variation, Maróczy Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 5..strategy: Threatens f5 to trap the bishop in the same way as the h-pawn does, but at a higher price: the pawn leaves f2, so e3 loses its guard and White's own kingside is thinner. Black parries the threat with a sound developing move and has no reason to worry.

Gives the bishop the h7 square before h5 can trap it, and takes g5 away from White's pieces. Black accepts that White gains space on the wing and keeps the bishop; the advanced h-pawn cramps Black's kingside but can also turn into a weakness later.

Meets the advance by blocking it: the pawn on h5 is defended by the bishop and the rook, so White cannot take it, and the bishop keeps its diagonal. The cost is a loosened kingside and the g5 square for White's pieces.
Develops, but the bishop on g6 is trapped once the h-pawn advances: the pawn on h7 blocks its retreat and every other square is covered. White wins a piece for a pawn.

Steps out of the way, protected by the f7 and h7 pawns, and keeps the bishop on its diagonal towards d3. White's knight is left offside on g5 with nothing to attack, so Black can drive it back and finish development without trouble.

Supports the bishop on f5 and opens the queen's diagonal to the knight on g5, which only the bishop on c1 guards. Black gets a solid centre and frees the king's bishop, at the price of a pawn on e6 that the knight keeps eyeing.

Develops the knight but leaves the bishop on f5 unprotected, so Qf3 attacks it at once and Black must spend the next move on its safety. The knight on g5 stays active meanwhile, eyeing f7 and h7. Playable, but White gains time.

Brings the second knight into play to support the advanced one: it guards g5 and covers e5, so the knight keeps eyeing f7 and h7 with good backing. White develops with a purpose and keeps pressure on the kingside; Black will challenge the advanced knight, but White has developed a piece meanwhile.

Threatens h5 to drive the bishop off g6 and begins a kingside pawn advance that brings the rook into play. Black attacks the knight in turn, so White gains space but spends more time on the kingside than on development.

Offers to trade the light-squared bishops, which relieves Black of the piece that has been moved twice. The exchange costs White the bishop's diagonal and leaves the knight on g5 with little to do. Sound but harmless, and Black finishes development easily.

Attacks the advanced knight at once and gains a tempo, and the pawn also gives the bishop a retreat on h7. The knight sacrifice on f7 does not work: the bishop simply takes it, leaving White a knight down for a pawn.
Frees the king's bishop and opens the queen's diagonal towards the knight on g5. The pawn on e6 is guarded by f7 and the bishop on g6 stays safe, which gives Black a solid, compact set-up.

Develops a piece and prepares to challenge the centre, but leaves White's advanced knight alone, so it keeps eyeing f7 and h7. White can use the time to trade it off or to build up. Playable, though a move behind the natural attack on the knight.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Karpov Variation, Modern Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..strategy: An aggressive try: the knight aims at f7 and e6 and tests Black's kingside from the start. Black must develop carefully and avoid loosening moves such as ...h6, since the pawn on f7 is guarded only by the king.

The calm way: it develops, covers g5 and d4 and offers to trade on f6, where Black can recapture with the other knight and keep the pawn structure intact. A slow manoeuvring game follows in which White keeps a small space edge.

Puts the bishop against f7 before the knight jumps to g5, a more patient way to pressure the kingside. The knight stays on e4 for the trade on f6, and Black can answer with calm development, so it asks fewer immediate questions.

Develops with a challenge to the knight on e4. If White exchanges, the knight on d7 recaptures and Black's pawn structure stays intact, which is the very reason for placing it there. Black develops comfortably while the bishop on c4 asks Black to look after f7.

Develops with the d7 knight, which opens the diagonal of the c8 bishop at once. If White trades on f6, the knight from g8 retakes and the pawn structure stays whole; the cost is that the g8 knight is still at home, so Black is a little behind in development.

Chases the bishop from its diagonal and frees the c8 bishop, but spends a second move with the same knight and puts it on a square where it does little for the centre. White's bishop simply retreats to b3, and Black has to make up the lost time.

Brings a second piece to bear on f7: the pawn is attacked by knight and bishop and defended only by the king, so Black has to react at once instead of developing freely. White takes the initiative, but if Black parries accurately the position is balanced.

Exchanges the knight that challenges the centre and keeps the bishop aimed at f7. The trade also eases Black's cramped development, so White's edge is small: this is a calm line in which White hopes for a little more space and an easy game.

Steps back out of the attack of the f6 knight and keeps the knights on, covering f5 and h5 while the bishop on c4 stays aimed at f7. White avoids the exchange but spends yet another move with the same piece, so Black completes development without trouble.

Blocks the bishop's diagonal to f7 and so meets the double attack at its root, while freeing the king's bishop. Black gets a solid centre and quick kingside development, but has to keep an eye on e6, which White's bishop and knight both attack.

Attacks the bishop but ignores the threat to f7, which bishop and knight attack and only the king guards. Bxf7+ wins the pawn with check and drives the king to d7, where it has lost the right to castle.
Hits the knight but forgets f7: Nxf7 forks queen and rook, and with the bishop on c4 the king cannot take the knight. Black loses material at once and has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Karpov Variation, Tiviakov-Fischer Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..strategy: The recapture with the knight keeps the pawn structure intact and clears the bishop on c8, which can now come out. The knight on f6 covers d5 and e4 and holds the centre: Black has a sound position, White slightly more space.

Recaptures with the pawn, doubling the f-pawns and opening the e-file against a king still in the centre: Qe2+ comes with a tempo. Black gets quick development in return for the worse structure, so this is playable, but clearly inferior to the knight recapture.

Doubles the f-pawns and breaks the pawns Black would castle behind, so the king has no safe home on the kingside. The open g-file gives the rook some play, but the pawn on f7 stays under the bishop's fire, and the damage seldom pays off.

Develops the second knight and invites the trade, which Black can answer by retaking with the knight and keeping the pawn structure whole: the point of 4...Nd7. Black stays solid and can challenge the white centre later with ...c5.

Develops with the d7 knight so the bishop on c8 has its diagonal open at once. If White trades on f6, the knight from g8 retakes and the pawn structure stays whole; the cost is that the g8 knight is still undeveloped.

Prepares to develop the king's bishop and keeps the pawn structure compact, but leaves White's knight on e4 undisturbed and the bishop on c8 shut in behind the knight on d7. Solid and slow: White is free to bring out the pieces and claim more space.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Karpov Variation, Modern Variation, Kasparov Attack
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..strategy: Retreats the knight instead of trading it on f6, keeping the pieces on for a kingside attack. From g3 it covers f5 and h5, so White presses for the initiative while Black has a solid position and must defend the kingside with care.

Trades the strong knight on e4 for the one that challenged it, and Black recaptures with the knight, so the structure stays whole. White keeps a small space advantage and an easy, risk-free game, while Black has no weaknesses to worry about.

Develops the bishop and defends the knight on e4, but the bishop is not a stable protector: Black can take on e4 and, after the recapture, develop the other knight to f6 with tempo against the bishop. White gets a normal game but loses time.

Develops the knight, covers h7 against the knight on g5 and prepares to drive that knight back. The knight on d7 still blocks the bishop on c8, so e6 and f7 need care: White's pieces aim at both, and Black must not loosen the kingside carelessly.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Karpov Variation, Modern Variation, Ivanchuk Defence
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5..strategy: Develops with the d7 knight instead, which opens the c8 bishop's diagonal at once: the bishop then defends e6, the square White's knight eyes. Black keeps the g8 knight at home and is a little behind in development, but the position is solid and ready to drive the knight back.

Prepares to develop the king's bishop, but the bishop on c8 stays shut in behind the knight on d7, and the pawns on e6 and f7 are targets for the knight on g5. White can pile up on e6, which only the f7 pawn guards, so Black has to defend with care.

Develops the bishop onto the diagonal towards h7, where it joins the knight on g5: the pawn is attacked twice, but Black's knight and rook defend it twice. White prepares to castle and keeps the initiative, with the knights ready to jump in if Black loosens the position.

Brings the bishop to the diagonal aimed at f7, which the knight on g5 also hits: Black has to answer the double attack at once, usually by blocking with a pawn on e6. White gains time and the initiative, but if Black blocks accurately the position is balanced.

Brings the queen out to cover e4, so the knight on g5 can retreat there if Black attacks it, and eyes the e-file. It develops no minor piece, so Black catches up in development; sound, but it does not ask much of Black.

Builds a solid structure and frees the king's bishop, accepting that the bishop on c8 stays shut in for now. The pawn on e6 and the f7 square are sensitive spots that White's knights aim at, so Black has to avoid weakening the kingside carelessly.

Drives at the knight but loosens the kingside: with the bishop on c8 blocked, Ne6 forks queen and bishop, and taking the knight with the f-pawn even loses to Bg6 mate. Black can defend with accurate play, but this walks a tightrope that a pawn on e6 avoids.

Frees the c8 bishop by moving the d7 knight away, so the bishop can come to f5 or g4 and challenge White's. The price is a second move with the same knight and a slower fight for the centre, while h7 stays guarded only by the f6 knight and the rook.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Trades off Black's active knight and forces a pawn recapture, which damages Black's pawn structure for good. White gets no quick attack but a lasting structural edge and the easier game: Black must make up for it with piece activity.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Alekhine Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: The gambit offers the d4 pawn for rapid development: after the queen takes it, Nf3 attacks the queen and gains time. White gives up a central pawn for tempi that Black can answer with calm development, so it is risky rather than sound.

Moves a developed knight for the third time to eye f7, in the hope that Black meets it with ...h6 and falls into a sacrifice. Black can simply develop or chase the knight, and White has lost time and gained nothing.

Challenges the knight at once. If it retreats, White has wasted time with a developed piece and Black stands comfortably; if it takes on f7, the sacrifice is unsound and Black simply captures the knight.

Develops the bishop before closing the centre, but leaves it unprotected, so Qf3 attacks it at once and Black has to retreat or defend it. The knight on g5 stays active meanwhile, so White gains time for the cost of an early queen move.

Develops a piece and supports the knight on f6, but shuts in the bishop on c8 and leaves White's knight in place, where it keeps pressing on f7 and h7. Black is solid, yet White has gained the initiative for the moment.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Alien Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..background: A knight sacrifice first played by Witty Alien, a streamer from Bulgaria.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Sacrifices a knight for a single pawn in the hope of hunting the black king. After ...Kxf7 the attack runs out: Black blocks the checks and keeps the extra piece, so the gambit works only against careless defence.

The sensible retreat: the knight returns to f3, where it develops, guards d4 and keeps the centre intact. White has spent two moves with the same piece, so Black is a little ahead, but nothing is lost; the sacrifice on f7 only loses a piece.

Steps back to the rim: the knight is out of danger but badly placed. If Black trades it for the bishop on c8, White gets the bishop pair at the price of doubled h-pawns and a weakened kingside; otherwise the knight needs a second move to find a useful square.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Tartakower Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..background: Also known as the Korchnoi Variation: Viktor Korchnoi played it many times, including in his first world championship match with Anatoly Karpov, and Ulf Andersson has also employed it.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: The sounder recapture: the e-pawn opens the f8-bishop and gives Black quick development. The price is doubled f-pawns and the white advantage in structure and long-term prospects, so Black has to play actively and avoid a slow endgame.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Bronstein-Larsen Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..background: David Bronstein and Bent Larsen employed it with some success, which gave it its name; Larsen used it widely in the 1970s.
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Opens the g-file for the rook and aims for active, unusual counterplay, but ruins the kingside pawns and practically forces Black to castle queenside. It gains dynamism at the cost of structure, and is generally considered somewhat unsound.

Supports d4 and gives the queen the c2 square, so White keeps a solid centre and the better structure. With the bishop coming to d3, White plays for a lasting edge against the doubled pawns without taking risks.

1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..name: Caro–Kann Defence: Forgacs Variation
1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5..strategy: Puts the bishop on its active diagonal at once, looking at f7, instead of supporting d4 first. Black answers with normal development, and White's structural edge is no quicker to reach, so it is a sound, less common way to play for a small advantage.

Develops the knight to its natural square, where it guards d4 and eyes e5, and leaves the pawn structure alone. White heads for a quiet game with castling and a bishop on d3, playing for the small edge that Black's doubled f-pawns give.

Develops the bishop to its best square: it covers the kingside, eyes h2 and prepares castling. Black accepts the doubled pawns for a harmonious position and uses the open lines for piece play, which is the point of the line.

Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, but gives up the guard of b7, so Qb3 asks an immediate question. Black can answer with ...Qb6, though trading queens would damage the queenside pawns, and a trade of bishops on d3 costs Black the more active piece.

Develops the bishop behind its pawns, where it guards f6 and prepares castling. Safe but passive: it gives up the active diagonal towards h2, so White gets an easy game with a lasting structural edge.
